results.summary_before: This design is a Bluetooth Low Energy digital baseband receiver for the SCuM single-chip micro-mote platform, taking I/Q samples and performing GFSK matched filtering, clock and data recovery, preamble detection and packet decoding with de-whitening and CRC checking. It is tested by connecting the SCuM RF front-end I/Q outputs, configuring it to receive BLE packets, and observing decoded data through the Tiny Tapeout output interface with a Digital Discovery and computer. External hardware includes the SCuM chip, a Digital Discovery for probing and a computer for serial communication and logging. The project is a large 3x4-tile SystemVerilog wireless receiver with detailed processing-stage documentation.

results.summary_before: TinyQV is a small RV32EC RISC-V SoC that executes code from external QSPI flash and uses QSPI PSRAM for data memory, with peripherals including UART, SPI, gamepad, PWM, CORDIC and others contributed by the Tiny Tapeout community. It is used by loading a program image into flash and following a specific reset and clocking sequence, with MicroPython scripts on the RP2040 demo board handling the setup. External hardware includes a QSPI PMOD with flash and RAM, a UART connection to the demo board, and optional buttons on the GPIO inputs. Silicon testers have confirmed MicroPython boots and runs at up to 59 MHz, though some peripherals have issues at high clock speeds, and the CORDIC core only converges within about ±99.9 degrees.

results.summary_before: Dog Battle Game is a VGA display engine that renders four animated colored boxes bouncing around a 640x480 screen with a simple physics simulation including friction, elastic collisions and wall bouncing. It runs continuously at 60 FPS on power-up and requires only a VGA monitor connected to the output pins, with no other external hardware or input needed. The design is a small 1x1 tile Verilog project that outputs 2-bit-per-channel RGB plus HS and VS sync signals. No silicon test report is provided, so the actual hardware behaviour is not documented.

results.summary_before: This is a framebuffer-less VGA ray casting engine inspired by Wolfenstein 3D that renders textured walls, optional doors and flat floor and ceiling by racing the beam, with player point-of-view and effect registers controlled over a single SPI interface. It is used by supplying a 21-31.5 MHz clock, attaching a Tiny VGA PMOD, and optionally driving the SPI interface or using the inc_px and inc_py inputs for a demo without an SPI host. External hardware includes a Tiny VGA PMOD, optional SPI controller and optional external QSPI ROM for textures, with a pin selecting between Leo Moser and Digilent QSPI PMODs. The design is an experimental GF180 port of earlier TT07 and TTCAD25a versions, and the documentation notes that testing instructions are still to be completed.

results.summary_before: This is a digital desk clock that keeps hours, minutes and seconds and drives a six-digit 7-segment display through a MAX7219 over SPI because there are not enough output pins to drive the segments directly. The time is set with hours_set and minutes_set inputs, with a fast/slow select input controlling the increment rate, and pressing both set inputs clears the seconds. It requires a 5 MHz clock, a 32.768 kHz reference clock on the refclk pin, and a MAX7219 7-segment display connected to the bidirectional PMOD. The design is a rehardening of a test design from Skywater and IHP processes for GF180, and no silicon test report is included.

results.summary_before: This project is a GF180 implementation of the bad synchronizer example from Dally and Harting, which passes a counter value between two clock domains through multiple register stages to demonstrate synchronization failures. It is used by aligning and then separating the two clocks and observing bit errors on the stage outputs, with an input selecting binary or Gray code counting. External hardware is a way to generate a clock, and the design exposes stage1, stage2 and stage3 outputs plus a skew signal. The documentation is intentionally brief and describes the design as working badly, since the point is to illustrate a known bad synchronization practice.
